property_summary: For every interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true from supportsInterface whenever interfaceId equals IAccessControl (regardless of ERC165 support), but the mutant returns false for some such interfaceIds because it requires both equality and super.supportsInterface to be true.

For any interfaceId, the reference contract returns true from supportsInterface whenever interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (it requires only that equality), while the mutant additionally requires super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) causing some calls with that interfaceId to return false — the property: supportsInterface(interfaceId)==true whenever interfaceId equals IAccessControl's id.

For every bytes4 input, the reference contract's supportsInterface returns true whenever the input equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant breaks this by additionally requiring super.supportsInterface(interfaceId), so it can return false for that same input.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference returns true when interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant can return false for that same interfaceId because it (incorrectly) also requires super.supportsInterface(interfaceId).

For all bytes4 interfaceId inputs, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true whenever interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant returns false for some such interfaceId because it (incorrectly) additionally requires super.supportsInterface(interfaceId).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract returns supportsInterface(interfaceId) == (interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId || super supportsInterface(interfaceId)), while the mutant inverts the first comparison causing some interfaceId (not equal to IAccessControl) to incorrectly return true; equivalently, the reference never returns true for an interfaceId that is neither IAccessControl nor supported by super, but the mutant can.

For every interfaceId the reference C returns true only if interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true; the mutant wrongly returns true whenever interfaceId != type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (making some previously-false interfaceIds true).

For every bytes4 id, the correct contract returns true only when id == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or super.supportsInterface(id) is true; the mutant instead returns true for some ids that are neither IAccessControl nor supported by super, so there exists an id where supportsInterface differs between reference and mutant.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C returns true iff interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true; the mutant instead returns true whenever interfaceId != type(IAccessControl).interfaceId, so there exist interfaceIds (not equal to IAccessControl and not supported by super) for which reference returns false but mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 id, C.supportsInterface(id) returns true only if id == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or ERC165.supportsInterface(id) is true; the mutant inverts the first equality and therefore can return true for ids that are neither IAccessControl nor supported by ERC165.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract C returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) exactly when interfaceId equals IAccessControl or IERC165 (i.e., C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) == (interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId || interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId)); the mutant always delegates to super and thus will return false for IAccessControl and so violate this rule for some interfaceId (namely IAccessControl).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (in addition to IERC165), but the mutant that returns super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) will return false for the IAccessControl interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (IAccessControl) for which the mutant differs.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true if and only if interfaceId == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId or interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant that only returns super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) will return false for IAccessControl.interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (the IAccessControl id) where return values differ.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true when interfaceId equals the IAccessControl interface id (in addition to IERC165), while the mutant that always returns super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) will return false for the IAccessControl id — so C.supportsInterface(type(IAccessControl).interfaceId) is true for all inputs whereas the mutant yields false for that input.

For every bytes4 id, the reference C.supportsInterface(id) returns true when id == type(IAccessControl).interfaceId (or when id == type(IERC165).interfaceId), but the mutant that delegates only to super.supportsInterface will return false for the IAccessControl id, so there exists an interface id (the IAccessControl id) where the mutant's return differs from the reference; the test asserts that calling supportsInterface with a fuzzed bytes4 that equals type(IAccessControl).interfaceId returns true (a property true for the reference but violated by the mutant).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct contract returns true iff the interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (as implemented by supportsInterface chaining), whereas the mutant returns true for all interfaceIds; thus there exist interfaceIds for which reference supportsInterface returns false but mutant returns true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true only when interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (as per ERC165 chaining); the mutant that always returns true violates this by returning true for some interfaceIds where the reference returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface either returns true only for supported interface IDs (IERC165 and IAccessControl via ERC165 chaining) or false otherwise; the mutant that always returns true will return true for some interfaceId values where the reference returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the correct C.supportsInterface call never returns true for arbitrary random ids that are not IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e. there exist ids for which correct returns false), while the mutant always returns true — so assert that for any fuzzed id if C.supportsInterface(id) returns true then id must equal one of the known supported interface ids (IERC165 or IAccessControl); the mutant will violate this for some fuzzed ids.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never returns true for interfaceIds other than IERC165 or IAccessControl (via ERC165 chaining); the mutant that always returns true will return true for some interfaceId where the reference returns false.

For any interfaceId, the correct contract's supportsInterface may return true for some ids (specifically it returns true for IERC165 and IAccessControl IDs), whereas the mutant always returns false, so there exists an interfaceId (fuzzed) for which the reference returns true but the mutant returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract's supportsInterface never reverts and returns true when interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl (i.e., returns true for at least those two well-known ids), while the mutant that always returns false will return false for those ids — so there exist fuzzed interfaceId values (specifically the ERC165/IAccessControl ids) where reference returns true but mutant returns false.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the correct contract never reverts; moreover there exists an interfaceId (specifically the IERC165 interface id) for which the correct contract returns true but the mutant always returns false, so the property is: supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) returns true (reference) while the mutant returns false.

For every bytes4 id the reference contract's supportsInterface never reverts and in particular returns true for the IERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId); the mutant that always returns false will return false for that id, so the universal property is: calling supportsInterface(i) never reverts and for i == type(IERC165).interfaceId the result is true.

For every bytes4 interfaceId input, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the correct contract never reverts, and in particular returns true when the fuzzed interfaceId equals the IERC165 interface id (the buggy mutant always returns false and thus will disagree for that input).
